when: a change handles a corner case or failure by adding new control mechanism (tunables, thresholds, latched or sticky state flags, grace windows, or layered special-case branches) instead of fixing the semantics that produce the corner case, especially when those branches need long comments to justify them
expect: Ask the author to justify each added knob, flag or special case. Ask them to look first for the minimal root-cause fix, such as reclassifying an ambiguous or missing result so the special case disappears. Ask them to restate the logic from first principles as one clear rule that can be said in a sentence and that the code visibly implements. Ask them to delete any mechanism that exists only to patch around the unclear semantics.
why: Extra state and thresholds multiply interacting cases that are hard to reason about and can hide the real bug. AI-assisted code tends to accumulate these layers. A direct semantic fix is easier to verify and maintain.
examples: Heartbeat tracking added a cold-start failure threshold and a 'first success seen' latch around missing ping responses. The reviewer called this possible over-design. Treating a None response from send_ping as a failed ping (False) removes the need for both.
A health tracker with grace windows, latched flags and multi-branch summaries was judged unnecessarily complicated. It can be reduced to the rule 'a failed ping marks the instance unhealthy'.
concern: Avoid over-designed control logic; prefer the minimal root-cause fix over added thresholds, latches and grace special cases

when: a change touches how the multiprocess server handles a KV-cache registration for an instance ID that is already registered, whether in the registration handler itself or in a re-registration, restart or recovery path
expect: Check that registering an already-registered instance ID is an idempotent no-op that keeps the existing GPU cache context and its handles. The change must not unregister, tear down, re-create or reset that context on a duplicate registration.
why: After a transient health-check failure, the engine side can legitimately send a duplicate registration. Rebuilding the GPU cache context, including its CUDA IPC handles, is slow. The no-op semantics were set deliberately when restart support was added.
examples: A PR made a duplicate registration unregister and rebuild the GPUCacheContext. The reviewer pointed to PR #3208 (support LMCache restart), which defined the case as a no-op when the instance ID already exists, because vLLM may re-register after a transient PING failure.
concern: Duplicate registration must be an idempotent no-op that keeps the existing context

when: a design document is added or revised and contains intermediate planning, step-by-step narration of explored alternatives, or 'thought process' text alongside or instead of a description of the resulting design
expect: Ask the author to keep only the final design: what it is, how it works, and the key decisions, with a brief rationale for each. Ask them to remove planning steps, abandoned explorations and reasoning narration.
why: Readers need the design as built. Planning narration, common in AI-generated drafts, buries the actual design and goes stale as the design evolves.
examples: A design doc contained 'quite a few intermediate AI-generated planning details'. The reviewer asked to keep only the description of the final design and drop the thought processes.
concern: Design docs describe only the final design, without planning or thought-process narration

when: A change adds a fallback path, degraded mode, or backward-compatibility guard for a condition the project's own invariants rule out. Examples are a hard-required dependency being absent, or a peer running a different version when the project always ships both sides together.
expect: Ask the author to name a real deployment that reaches the branch. If none exists, ask them to remove the fallback or compat branch, call the required path unconditionally, and assume the current contract on every side.
why: Branches for conditions that cannot occur are untested dead code. They add maintenance surface and can hide real misconfiguration that should fail loudly instead.
examples: A pure-Python or legacy fallback for when the compiled `lmcache.c_ops` extension is missing in MP cache engine code. The GPU kernels cannot work without the extension, so the fallback is never a working configuration.
Backward-compatibility guards in the serving-engine-side adapter for an older LMCache server. LMCache controls both client and server, and they always ship at the same version.
concern: No defensive fallback or compat paths for conditions that cannot occur (hard requirements, same-version peers)

when: A change introduces a new config option, flag, or field whose value is already determined by one or more existing fields, such as whether an optional path or name is set.
expect: Ask the author to drop the new option and derive the state from the existing fields. Validation and conflict checks should be written directly against those fields, for example raising when two mutually exclusive fields are both set.
why: Redundant flags can disagree with the fields they duplicate, and they enlarge the config surface that users must keep consistent.
examples: A new `l1_use_shm` boolean was added although an empty or non-empty `shm_name` already says whether SHM is in use. The conflict check should be `if self.devdax_path and self.shm_name: raise`.
concern: Derive state from existing fields instead of adding redundant config flags

when: A change adds or calls a native op that only some device backends implement, or adds a capability flag, placeholder type, or base-class stub to signal whether a backend supports an op.
expect: The base device ops interface should declare only ops that every backend implements. Backend-specific ops belong only in the per-device ops modules of the backends that support them. Callers should detect support with a plain `hasattr` check on the ops module. Ask the author to remove placeholder stub types, base-class stubs, and module-level capability flags that exist only to signal support.
why: The device ops layer is designed for per-device specialized functions. Stubs or flags in the base interface duplicate what `hasattr` already reports, and they leak backend specifics into the generic layer.
examples: `execute_object_group_transfer` is CUDA/AMD-only but was placed in `base_device_ops.py`, along with a `NativePlanType` stub and a capability flag that inspected it. The fix was to keep the op in the CUDA/AMD ops modules, remove the stub and the flag, and check `hasattr(ops, "execute_object_group_transfer")`.
concern: Backend-specific native ops live in per-device modules, detected via hasattr
